profile.name: Electric-Techno Neon Gods
profile.tagline: Taiwanese folk dance fuses temple tradition with electronic beats and LED-lit costumes
profile.insight: In 2009, Electric-Techno Neon Gods danced at the World Games, blending temple deity costumes with techno music and LED lights.
profile.profile: Electric-Techno Neon Gods is a Taiwanese dance merging traditional temple procession dances with modern techno music. Originating from Yunlin or Chiayi counties, young dancers in deity bodyguard costumes perform dynamic movements to electronic rhythms. Costumes mix traditional elements with LED lights and sunglasses, reflecting a vibrant fusion of folk religion and pop culture. The dance appears at religious festivals and major international events, symbolizing contemporary Taiwanese identity.
profile.profile_long:
Electric-Techno Neon Gods (Chinese: 電音三太子; pinyin: Diànyīn Sāntàizi) is a distinctive Taiwanese dance form that combines the traditional folk temple procession dance known as zhèntóu (陣頭) with modern electronic and techno music. The dance centers around the figure of Nezha, the Third Prince (San Taizi), a popular deity in Taiwanese folk religion. Its origins are debated, with some sources tracing it to Beigang Township in Yunlin County and others to Puzi City in Chiayi County. Initially, local temple groups featured performers dressed as divine bodyguards (大仙尪仔) who danced during religious parades. These performers, often young men, began incorporating their favorite club music—disco and techno—into the traditional movements, creating a hybrid style that energized temple festivities and attracted younger audiences.

The dancers wear elaborate costumes inspired by traditional deity attire but updated with contemporary accessories like oversized sunglasses, white gloves, and LED lights. The white gloves are a popular dance accessory in Taiwan. The demanding choreography requires strength and endurance, as the performers carry heavy, often oversized costumes and masks. Over time, professional dance troupes specializing in Electric-Techno Neon Gods have emerged, performing not only at religious events but also at secular and international venues. Notably, the dance featured in the opening ceremonies of the 2009 World Games, the 2009 Summer Deaflympics, Expo 2010 Shanghai, and the 2010 Taipei International Flora Exposition.

Musically, the dance is performed to modern techno rhythms, including original compositions by procession participants and popular disco tracks. A key musical influence is the Taike dance style, which is integral to most Electric-Techno Neon Gods performances. The dance exemplifies a unique cultural synthesis, blending Taiwanese folk religion with global pop culture elements to express a modern Taiwanese identity. It remains a living tradition, vibrant in both religious and secular contexts.

The dance's formation typically involves groups of dancers embodying the deity's entourage, moving in procession or choreographed sequences. The tempo is energetic, matching the electronic beats. Signature costume elements and dance gestures highlight the fusion of old and new, sacred and popular. The dance is not described as sacred or restricted, allowing public performance at various events. This blend of tradition and innovation makes Electric-Techno Neon Gods a compelling example of cultural continuity and adaptation in Taiwan.

sections.origins_and_history: Electric-Techno Neon Gods originated in Taiwan, with two main theories placing its birth in Beigang Township, Yunlin County, or Puzi City, Chiayi County. It evolved from traditional temple procession dances where performers dressed as divine bodyguards accompanied deities. Young dancers introduced electronic music to the traditional choreography, creating a new hybrid dance form that gained popularity beyond religious rituals. Professional troupes now perform it at both temple festivals and international events.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers wear traditional deity bodyguard costumes enhanced with LED lights and accessories like oversized sunglasses and white gloves. The dance involves dynamic, energetic movements requiring strength and endurance to manage heavy costumes. Performers move in groups, often in procession formations, alternating traditional steps with techno rhythms. The tempo is fast, matching electronic music beats. Technique not described in sources in detail.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music combines modern techno rhythms with traditional Taiwanese procession sounds. Performances use original techno compositions and popular disco tracks, including Korean dance music influences. The Taike dance style is a core musical element, often present in performances. Instruments are electronic, with synthesized beats and bass lines typical of techno music.
sections.costume_and_setting: Costumes are based on traditional Taiwanese deity bodyguard attire, featuring colorful, oversized, and often heavy garments and masks. Modern elements include LED lights, oversized sunglasses, and white gloves. The dance is performed during temple festivals, religious parades, and large secular events such as the 2009 World Games and Expo 2010 Shanghai.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Originally part of religious temple processions honoring deities, the dance now appears at secular and international events, symbolizing modern Taiwanese cultural identity. It bridges folk religion and contemporary pop culture, appealing to both traditional audiences and youth. The dance serves as a cultural ambassador for Taiwan at global gatherings.
sections.lineage: Electric-Techno Neon Gods descends from traditional Taiwanese temple procession dances (zhèntóu) featuring deity bodyguards. It incorporates modern techno and disco music, influenced by Taike dance styles, creating a unique fusion distinct to Taiwan.

claims.text: Electric-Techno Neon Gods is a subcultural dance performance which combines a traditional Taiwan folk dance performance with modern pop music.
claims.quote: Electric-Techno Neon Gods ... combines a traditional Taiwan folk dance performance ... with modern pop music.

claims.text: The dance originated either from Beigang Township, Yunlin County, or Puzi City, Chiayi County, Taiwan.
claims.quote: One says it is from Beigang Township, Yunlin County, Taiwan; while the other one says it started from Puzi City, Chiayi County, Taiwan.

claims.text: Performers dress as bodyguards of the gods and perform dances during religious parades at local temples.
claims.quote: Some people dressed up as bodyguards of the gods ... and performed similar dances during religious parades at local temples.

claims.text: Young dancers combined traditional dances with electronic music, leading to professional dance teams specializing in Electric-Techno Neon Gods.
claims.quote: As many of the dancers were young people who enjoyed going clubbing, they began combining the traditional dances with electronic music.

claims.text: Costumes mix traditional outfits with trendy elements like oversized sunglasses and LED lights; white gloves are commonly worn.
claims.quote: The costumes ... with trendy elements added ... such as oversized sunglasses and LED lights. White gloves are commonly worn.

claims.text: The dance was performed during the opening ceremonies of the World Games 2009, Deaflympics 2009, Expo 2010 Shanghai, and Taipei International Flora Exposition 2010.
claims.quote: Such dances were performed during the opening ceremonies of the World Games 2009, 2009 Summer Deaflympics, Expo 2010 Shanghai China, the 2010 Taipei International Flora Exposition.

claims.text: The dance is named after the Buddhist-Daoist deity Nezha, known as the Third Prince (San Taizi).
claims.quote: Der Name stammt von der buddhistisch-daoistischen Gottheit Nezha, der im Volksmund als „Dritter Prinz“ (chinesisch: San Taizi) bekannt ist.

claims.text: The dance evolved from performers representing divine bodyguards in colorful, oversized costumes and masks during Daoist processions.
claims.quote: Diese göttlichen Leibwachen-Figuren ... werden von eigens dafür trainierten Darstellern in farbenprächtigen, oft überlebensgroßen Kostümen und Masken dargestellt.

claims.text: Young men introduced disco and techno music into temple processions, alternating traditional and techno rhythms.
claims.quote: Man sagt, dass es junge Männer waren, die ... Disco- und Technomusik ... bei den Tempelprozessionen abwechselnd zu traditionellen und Techno-Rhythmen tanzten.

claims.text: The dance style has become a symbol of modern Taiwanese identity and is popular at religious and secular public events.
claims.quote: Der Tanz ... ist heute auf vielen öffentlichen Veranstaltungen religiösen wie nicht-religiösen Charakters populär.
